intro: A small C major tune, soft strings, then one outrageous chord from the whole orchestra. Haydn spends the rest of the Andante showing how much more there is to this tune than the joke.

cues.title: A tune on tiptoe
cues.text: The violins play a little C major tune, with the bass adding a note at the start of each bar. Its first phrase returns even more softly, with plucked strings. Then the whole orchestra hits a fortissimo G major chord.
cues.evidence: Andante, bars 1–16: the string theme, pianissimo pizzicato repeat and G major chord. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The tune gains a companion
cues.text: The second violins and violas keep the tune while the first violins weave semiquavers around it. A flute joins some of the answering phrases. The plain melody is still there, tucked beneath the decoration.
cues.evidence: Andante, first variation, bars 33–48: theme in second violins and violas, with first-violin and flute counterpoint. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Haydn wants to surprise London
cues.text: In Griesinger’s 1810 biography, Haydn explains his London ambition: “I wanted to surprise the public with something new.” His pupil Pleyel is writing for a rival concert series. Haydn means to make the stronger impression.
cues.evidence: Georg August Griesinger, Biographische Notizen über Joseph Haydn (1810), recollection of a conversation with Haydn. Our translation of “das Publikum durch etwas Neues zu überraschen”; German text reproduced at https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)

cues.title: C major turns minor
cues.text: The second variation strikes out in C minor. Loud unison phrases meet quiet strings; then the two violin sections answer each other through E♭ major and F minor. Haydn stretches the neat tune into a much less tidy conversation.
cues.evidence: Andante, second variation, bars 49–74: shortened opening, violin dialogue and E♭ major and F minor passages. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An oboe takes the tune
cues.text: C major returns with the oboe. Later the flute joins it in a duet, while the violins carry the familiar melody beneath the wind parts. The orchestra has become a small chamber ensemble.
cues.evidence: Andante, third variation, bars 75–106: oboe opening and the flute–oboe–violin combination. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The little tune marches
cues.text: The full orchestra plays the fourth variation fortissimo, with off-beat accompaniment. Then Haydn slips in a quiet passage for strings and bassoon, marked piano, before the grand manner returns.
cues.evidence: Andante, fourth variation, bars 107–138; quiet strings and bassoon at bars 115–130. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Strange chords under familiar notes
cues.text: In the coda, the winds bring back the simple tune above held string chords. Sevenths and ninths cloud the harmony while C stays in the bass. Haydn has saved his gentlest surprise for the end.
cues.evidence: Andante, coda from bar 139: seventh and ninth chords above a C pedal. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn). Wind melody and altered string harmonies: https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-94-surprise
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Semiquavers grow around the tune
transitions.from: Theme · Quiet strings, one startling chord
transitions.to: Var 1 · First violins embroider the tune
transitions.how: The theme closes in C major. A fresh orchestral chord launches the first variation, then the second violins and violas take the melody while the first violins add running semiquavers. The bass keeps the same harmonic route and the Andante pulse continues.
transitions.evidence: Andante, bars 32–48: first-variation scoring and counterpoint. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)

transitions.title: C stays while E falls
transitions.from: Var 1 · First violins embroider the tune
transitions.to: Var 2 · C minor, loud and terse
transitions.how: C major changes to C minor: E♭ replaces E♮ above the same home note. The orchestra plays the opening phrase loudly in unison, then quiet strings supply a shortened answer. Haydn cuts together the beginning and ending of the original tune.
transitions.evidence: Andante, second variation from bar 49: mode change and compression of the theme’s two halves. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)

transitions.title: The violins leave room for an oboe
transitions.from: Var 2 · C minor, loud and terse
transitions.to: Var 3 · Oboe, then a flute duet
transitions.how: A falling first-violin figure leads out of the minor variation. The next statement restores C major and places the tune in the first oboe above strings. Flute and oboe later add their own parts over the melody in the violins.
transitions.evidence: Andante, end of second variation and third variation, bars 74–106. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)

transitions.title: The orchestra takes over
transitions.from: Var 3 · Oboe, then a flute duet
transitions.to: Var 4 · A march for the orchestra
transitions.how: The wind-led variation closes in C major. The fourth begins in the same key and tempo, now fortissimo for the full orchestra, with syncopated accompaniment. Trumpets and timpani join the strings and winds for the tune’s march-like opening.
transitions.evidence: Andante, bars 106–114: C major cadence and full-orchestra fourth variation. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)

transitions.title: A held C, changing chords
transitions.from: Var 4 · A march for the orchestra
transitions.to: Coda · Winds above a held C
transitions.how: After the final variation, the coda recalls the tune in the winds. The strings hold seventh and ninth chords beneath it while C remains in the bass. The melody keeps its simple outline; the sustained chords change the sound of its familiar notes.
transitions.evidence: Andante, coda from bar 139, https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn); Orrin Howard’s description of wind melody and string harmonies, https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-94-surprise

source.title: Haydn, Symphony No. 94, full score (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, ed. Rietz, plate 8876, [1855])
source.locator: Andante, printed pp. 19–29: theme, four variations and coda.

timeline.note: The strings play the quiet tune; its first phrase returns still softer and plucked.
The whole orchestra strikes the fortissimo G major chord.
Flute and oboe join the violin tune; horns hold soft notes beneath them.
The first violins decorate the tune in second violins and violas; flute joins the answering phrases.
The strings continue the first variation on their own.
Winds and strings strike out fortissimo in C minor.
Trumpets and timpani join the C minor climax while the horns rest.
The oboe brings back C major above bassoons and semiquavers in the violins.
Flute and oboe play a duet above the tune in the violins.
Soft held horn notes support the flute and oboe.
The fourth variation starts fortissimo, with brass, timpani and running violin scales.
Strings and bassoons answer the loud orchestra, piano dolce.
Tremolo strings lead the crescendo to a fortissimo chord held under a fermata.
The winds recall the tune above held string chords and a C in the bass.

quote.text: The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I.
quote.source: London notebook, after his benefit concert on 4 May 1795; our translation

composer.background:
On 4 May 1795, Haydn gave a benefit concert at the King’s Theatre in London. The programme included his new D major Symphony, now numbered 104. Afterwards he entered the result in his notebook: “The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I. I made four thousand gulden this evening. Such a thing can only be done in England.” He was sixty-three, a wheelwright’s son who had spent most of his adult life wearing an Esterházy servant’s livery.

Haydn was born in Rohrau in 1732. His father made wheels, played the harp by ear and sang; his mother had worked as a cook. At about six, Joseph left home for schooling in Hainburg. By 1740 he was a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. Singing gave him a daily education in church music, though little instruction in composition. It also gave him chances to find a meal at performances outside the cathedral. When his voice broke and he was dismissed in 1749, another musician, Johann Michael Spangler, took him into his family’s crowded room.
